title: Performance Optimization Guide
text:
This document explains the performance optimizations applied to your Quarto website.


To build and optimize your website:
./build.sh
Or manually:
quarto render
python3 optimize_html.py



The optimize_html.py script automatically applies the following optimizations to all generated HTML files:



Non-critical scripts are moved to the end of the <body> tag with defer attribute
Critical scripts (quarto.js, bootstrap.min.js) remain in <head> but are deferred
This prevents scripts from blocking HTML parsing and rendering





Critical CSS files (Bootstrap, Bootstrap Icons, Syntax Highlighting) are preloaded
Browsers can start downloading CSS earlier, improving First Contentful Paint





preconnect hints added for external resources (e.g., GitHub)
Reduces DNS lookup and connection time for external resources





Scripts are ordered to ensure dependencies load correctly
Critical scripts load before dependent scripts





The optimization script includes performance monitoring that logs: - Page load start time - DOMContentLoaded event timing - Individual script load times - Resource load times and sizes - Window load completion time
Logs are written to .cursor/debug.log in NDJSON format.



After optimization, you should see: - Faster First Contentful Paint (FCP): CSS preloading and script deferral allow content to render sooner - Faster Time to Interactive (TTI): Scripts don’t block rendering - Better Lighthouse scores: Improved performance metrics - Reduced blocking time: Scripts load asynchronously without blocking the main thread




Before optimization: Run quarto render and test your site
After optimization: Run ./build.sh and test again
Compare: Use browser DevTools Network tab or Lighthouse to compare load times




After running the build script, commit and push the optimized files in the docs/ directory:
git add docs/
git commit -m "Optimize HTML for performance"
git push



If scripts don’t work after optimization: 1. Ensure scripts are loaded in the correct order 2. Check browser console for errors 3. Verify that deferred scripts don’t have dependencies on non-deferred scripts

build.sh: Build script that runs Quarto render + optimization
_quarto.yml: Updated with performance-related settings

text:
Complete Workflow

Step-by-Step: Generating a Bar Chart

Step 1: User Opens Application
Browser → GET http://localhost:5000/
    ↓
Program.cs (routing) → PlotController.Index()
    ↓
PlotController → return View()
    ↓
Views/Plot/Index.cshtml rendered
    ↓
HTML + JavaScript sent to browser


Step 2: User Clicks “Generate Plot”
Client-Side (JavaScript):
// 1. User clicks button
generateBtn.onclick = async function() {
    // 2. Prepare request
    const plotType = 'bar';
    
    // 3. Send POST request
    const response = await fetch('/Plot/Generate', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: `plotType=${plotType}`
    });
}


Step 3: Server Processes Request
Server-Side (C#):
Browser → POST /Plot/Generate?plotType=bar
    ↓
PlotController.Generate("bar")
    ↓
RPlotService.GeneratePlotAsync("bar", logCallback)
    ↓
Process.Start(Rscript.exe)
    ↓
Command: Rscript.exe "create_plots.R" "bar" "C:\...\wwwroot\plots\plot_bar_20251225.png"


Step 4: R Executes
R Process:
# 1. R receives arguments
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
# args[1] = "bar"
# args[2] = "C:\...\wwwroot\plots\plot_bar_20251225.png"

# 2. Create plot
p <- ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = class, fill = class)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(title = "Count of Vehicles by Class")

# 3. Save to file
ggsave(filename = args[2], plot = p)


Step 5: Response Returns to Browser
Server Response:
{
    "success": true,
    "plotUrl": "/plots/plot_bar_20251225_143022.png",
    "logs": "Generating bar plot...\n[R OUTPUT] Creating plot type: bar\n..."
}
Client-Side Display:
// 4. Receive response
const result = await response.json();

// 5. Display image
plotArea.innerHTML = `<img src="${result.plotUrl}" class="img-fluid">`;
// Browser requests: GET /plots/plot_bar_20251225_143022.png


Step 6: Browser Displays Plot
Browser → GET /plots/plot_bar_20251225_143022.png
    ↓
ASP.NET Core Static Files Middleware
    ↓
Serves file from wwwroot/plots/
    ↓
Image displayed in browser

Conclusion
The RPlotViewerWeb application demonstrates a clean separation of concerns:

Program.cs: Application configuration
PlotController: HTTP request handling
RPlotService: R integration and file management
create_plots.R: Statistical visualization logic
Index.cshtml: User interface

This architecture makes the application: - ✅ Maintainable: Each component has a single responsibility - ✅ Testable: Services can be mocked and tested independently - ✅ Extensible: New plot types require minimal changes - ✅ Scalable: Async operations prevent thread blocking
The key insight is treating R as an external service, communicating via process execution and file I/O, which provides a clean boundary between the .NET and R ecosystems.

Swift in Doom Emacs
text:
A practical guide to getting a full Swift/iOS development environment inside Doom Emacs.




macOS with Xcode installed
Doom Emacs configured
xcode-select --install already run





(let* ((dev   (string-trim (shell-command-to-string "xcode-select -p")))
       (sklsp (expand-file-name
               "Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/sourcekit-lsp" dev)))
  (setenv "DEVELOPER_DIR" dev)
  (setq lsp-sourcekit-executable sklsp
        lsp-sourcekit-extra-args  nil))
Why this works:
xcode-select -p returns the active developer directory (e.g. /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer). We dynamically derive the path to sourcekit-lsp from it rather than hardcoding, so it survives Xcode updates. Setting DEVELOPER_DIR in the environment ensures child processes (builds, LSP server) also know where the toolchain lives.




(setq lsp-ts-query-parser-install-directories
      ["/YOUR_HOME/.config/emacs/.local/cache/tree-sitter"])
Replace /YOUR_HOME with your home directory path, or use (expand-file-name "~/.config/emacs/.local/cache/tree-sitter").
Why this works:
Doom caches tree-sitter grammars here. Telling lsp-mode where they live enables richer semantic highlighting and navigation.




clone from here github in localpackages directory.
~/.config/doom/
└── localpackages/
    └── swift-development/
        ├── swift-development.el
        ├── xcode-project.el
        ├── xcode-build-config.el
        ├── ios-simulator.el
        ├── swift-refactor.el
        └── localizeable-mode.el
Then load them in your config.el:
(require 'transient)

(add-to-list 'load-path
             (expand-file-name "localpackages/swift-development" doom-private-dir))

(require 'swift-development)
(require 'xcode-project)
(require 'xcode-build-config)
(require 'ios-simulator)
(require 'swift-refactor)
(require 'localizeable-mode)
Why this works:
doom-private-dir points to your Doom config directory. Adding the subfolder to load-path lets Emacs find the .el files with require. transient is loaded first because the Swift modules use it for menu-driven commands (like Magit-style popups).




(map! :after (swift-mode swift-ts-mode)
      :map (swift-mode-map swift-ts-mode-map)
      :localleader
      "b" #'swift-development-compile-and-run
      "B" #'swift-development-compile-app
      "r" #'swift-development-run
      "i" #'swift-incremental-build-compile-and-run
      "t" #'swift-test-explorer-toggle
      "p" #'swiftui-preview-toggle)
Why this works:
:after defers binding until the mode is loaded, avoiding errors at startup. :localleader maps to , in Doom by default, so inside any Swift file you get:



Key
Action




, b
Compile and run


, B
Compile only


, r
Run


, i
Incremental build + run


, t
Toggle test explorer


, p
Toggle SwiftUI preview







This is an easy-to-miss but important step:
(setq process-environment
      (cl-remove-if
       (lambda (env)
         (string-match-p
          "^\\(LIBRARY_PATH\\|CPATH\\|C_INCLUDE_PATH\\|OBJC_INCLUDE_PATH\\)=" env))
       process-environment))
Why this works:
When Emacs is compiled with native compilation (libgccjit), it injects LIBRARY_PATH, CPATH, and related variables into its own environment. These leak into every subprocess — including Xcode builds and the Swift compiler — causing confusing linker errors like:
ld: warning: ignoring file ... unexpected architecture
Filtering them out before any build process runs keeps Xcode’s environment clean.




(map! :after swift-mode
      :map swift-mode-map
      :n [C-return] #'swift-mode:send-region)
Why this works:
In normal mode, C-RET sends the selected region to the Swift REPL. Great for quick experimentation without a full build cycle.




;;; --- Xcode Toolchain + SourceKit-LSP ---
(let* ((dev   (string-trim (shell-command-to-string "xcode-select -p")))
       (sklsp (expand-file-name
               "Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/sourcekit-lsp" dev)))
  (setenv "DEVELOPER_DIR" dev)
  (setq lsp-sourcekit-executable sklsp
        lsp-sourcekit-extra-args  nil))

;;; --- Tree-sitter Parser Cache ---
(setq lsp-ts-query-parser-install-directories
      ["/YOUR_HOME/.config/emacs/.local/cache/tree-sitter"])

;;; --- Fix Compiler Environment Leak ---
(setq process-environment
      (cl-remove-if
       (lambda (env)
         (string-match-p
          "^\\(LIBRARY_PATH\\|CPATH\\|C_INCLUDE_PATH\\|OBJC_INCLUDE_PATH\\)=" env))
       process-environment))

;;; --- Swift Development Packages ---
(require 'transient)
(add-to-list 'load-path
             (expand-file-name "localpackages/swift-development" doom-private-dir))

(require 'swift-development)
(require 'xcode-project)
(require 'xcode-build-config)
(require 'ios-simulator)
(require 'swift-refactor)
(require 'localizeable-mode)

;;; --- Keybindings ---
(map! :after (swift-mode swift-ts-mode)
      :map (swift-mode-map swift-ts-mode-map)
      :localleader
      "b" #'swift-development-compile-and-run
      "B" #'swift-development-compile-app
      "r" #'swift-development-run
      "i" #'swift-incremental-build-compile-and-run
      "t" #'swift-test-explorer-toggle
      "p" #'swiftui-preview-toggle)

(map! :after swift-mode
      :map swift-mode-map
      :n [C-return] #'swift-mode:send-region)




Make sure these are in your packages.el:
(package! swift-mode)
(package! lsp-sourcekit)
Then run doom sync and restart Emacs.

That’s it. Open any .swift file and LSP should start automatically, your local leader keys will be available, and your builds won’t be polluted by Emacs’s internal compiler paths.

title: R in Doom Emacs
text:
Supercharging R Development in Doom Emacs: A Reproducible Setup
Emacs Speaks Statistics (ESS) is the undisputed champion for R development, but configuring it to feel modern and fluid can be a task. If you are using Doom Emacs, you get a pre-configured base, but specific workflows require specific tweaks.
Here is why the configuration below works and how to reproduce it step-by-step.

Why This Works
This configuration solves three specific pain points: visual noise, process latency, and window chaos.

Speeding Up Evaluation: The line (setq ess-eval-visibly 'nowait) is crucial. By default, ESS waits for the R console to echo your code before returning control. This causes lag. 'nowait sends the code to the inferior process instantly, keeping your editing flow uninterrupted.
Taming Window Management: Doom Emacs uses shackle (via set-popup-rules!) to manage popups. ESS creates buffers like *R* (REPL) and *help[R]*. Without rules, these might steal your focus or split windows unpredictably. The rules defined here ensure the REPL sits neatly on the left and help buffers on the bottom, staying out of your way.
Aesthetic Cleanliness: We enable display-fill-column-indicator-mode visually but disable flymake to prevent heavy linting from freezing large files. We also define ess-indent-with-fancy-comments nil to stop ESS from aggressively re-indenting standard comments, which often breaks the flow of writing roxygen2 documentation.



How to Set This Up (Reproducibly)
This setup requires a small modification to your Doom configuration.
Step 1: Prerequisites Ensure you have the ess module enabled in your init.el or packages.el.
Step 2: The Configuration Add the following to your config.el (or ~/.doom.d/config.el). This isolates settings to load only when R is active, keeping your startup time fast.
;; --- Core ESS Settings ---
(after! ess-r-mode
  ;; 1. Visuals
  (add-hook! 'ess-r-mode-hook #'display-fill-column-indicator-mode)
  (setq ess-eval-visibly 'nowait)           : Faster evaluation
  (setq ess-use-flymake nil)                : Disable heavy linting
  (setq ess-ask-for-ess-directory nil)      : Don't prompt for working dir
  (setq ess-indent-with-fancy-comments nil) : Cleaner indentation logic
  (setq ess-style 'RStudio-)                : Follow RStudio style guide

  ;; 2. Fontification (Syntax Highlighting)
  (setq ess-R-font-lock-keywords
        '((ess-R-fl-keyword:keywords . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:constants . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:modifiers . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:fun-defs . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:assign-ops . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:%op% . t)
          (ess-fl-keyword:fun-calls . t)
          (ess-fl-keyword:numbers . t)
          (ess-fl-keyword:operators . t)
          (ess-fl-keyword:= . t)
          (ess-R-fl-keyword:F&T . t)))

  ;; 3. REPL Behavior
  (setq comint-move-point-for-output t)     : Auto-scroll REPL
  (add-hook! 'inferior-ess-mode-hook
    (lambda () (setq ansi-color-for-comint-mode 'filter)))
  (add-hook 'inferior-ess-mode-hook #'doom-mark-buffer-as-real-h)

  (set-popup-rules!
    '(("*R$" :side left :height 1 :width .5)   : Main REPL on left

      ("*help" :side bottom :height .5 :width .5)))) : Help docs on bottom

      :map ess-r-mode-map

title: Running Scheduled Tasks Without Cron: A Simple Bash-Based Scheduler
text:
A complete guide with examples, time customization, and process management
Sometimes you need to automate a task on a Linux server — but crontab isn’t available. This is common on restricted systems, containers, or environments where cron is not installed or disabled.
With a simple Bash loop, you can create your own lightweight scheduler that behaves similarly to cron.
This guide covers:

How to build a Bash-based scheduler
How to change the schedule time and day
Example scripts
Directory structure
How to start, stop, and restart the scheduler
Logging
Notes about server timezone differences


Note: The Linux server time may be different from your local timezone. Always verify the server time with:
date
Adjust the scheduled time accordingly.


Directory Structure
your-project/
│
├── master.sh
├── run_schedule.sh
└── scheduler.log        # created after first run


Example Task Script (master.sh)
This script is what you want to run on schedule.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Master script executed at $(date)" >> master.log


The Scheduler Script (run_schedule.sh)
This script continuously checks the date and time. It runs master.sh every Saturday at 06:00.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

SCRIPT="./master.sh"

while true; do
    DOW=$(date +%u)      # Day of week (1–7, Monday=1)
    TIME=$(date +%H:%M)  # Time in 24-hour format (HH:MM)

    if [[ "$DOW" == "6" && "$TIME" == "06:00" ]]; then
        echo "Running master.sh at $(date)"
        bash "$SCRIPT"
        sleep 60  # Prevent running twice in the same minute
    fi

    sleep 20
done


How to Change the Schedule (DOW & TIME)
The scheduler uses two conditions:

DOW → Day of week
TIME → Exact time (HH:MM)


Changing the Day of the Week (DOW)
The command date +%u returns:



Value
Day




1
Monday


2
Tuesday


3
Wednesday


4
Thursday


5
Friday


6
Saturday


7
Sunday




Examples
Run every Monday at 06:00:
if [[ "$DOW" == "1" && "$TIME" == "06:00" ]]; then
Run every Wednesday at 06:00:
if [[ "$DOW" == "3" && "$TIME" == "06:00" ]]; then
Run every Sunday at 06:00:
if [[ "$DOW" == "7" && "$TIME" == "06:00" ]]; then



Changing the Time (TIME)
Time is checked using:
TIME=$(date +%H:%M)
This is 24-hour format.

Examples
Run at 07:30 AM:
if [[ "$TIME" == "07:30" ]]; then
Run at 11:45 PM (23:45):
if [[ "$TIME" == "23:45" ]]; then
Run at midnight:
if [[ "$TIME" == "00:00" ]]; then



Running Twice in a Day
Example: Run at 06:00 and 18:00 on Saturday:
if [[ "$DOW" == "6" && ( "$TIME" == "06:00" || "$TIME" == "18:00" ) ]]; then


Running Every Day at a Specific Time
Remove the DOW check:
if [[ "$TIME" == "06:00" ]]; then


Running Every Hour at HH:00
if [[ "$(date +%M)" == "00" ]]; then



Running the Scheduler in Background
Give execute permissions:
chmod +x master.sh
chmod +x run_schedule.sh
Start it using nohup so it survives logout:
nohup ./run_schedule.sh > scheduler.log 2>&1 &


Checking If the Scheduler Is Running
pgrep -fl run_schedule.sh
Or:
ps aux | grep run_schedule.sh


Stopping (Killing) the Scheduler
Kill by name:
pkill -f run_schedule.sh
Or kill by process ID:
ps aux | grep run_schedule.sh
kill <PID>
Force kill:
kill -9 <PID>


Restarting the Scheduler
pkill -f run_schedule.sh
nohup ./run_schedule.sh > scheduler.log 2>&1 &


Viewing Logs
tail -f scheduler.log


Final Thoughts
This method lets you schedule tasks without relying on cron. By adjusting the DOW and TIME variables, you can create almost any schedule you want — daily tasks, weekly tasks, specific hours, or multiple run times.

title: fd command
text:
Install it on macOS and Windows, then bend it to your will with fzf, awk, cut, and sort.




Why fd instead of find
Installing fd

macOS
Windows
Verify the install

The mental model
Finding files
Finding directories
Acting on results: exec and xargs
fd + fzf: the pairing that ruins other file pickers for you
fd + awk
fd + cut
fd + sort and uniq
fd with everything else
Generating Markdown files
Windows and PowerShell notes
Cheat sheet





find is powerful, portable, and almost universally installed. It is also exhausting to type:
# find: files modified in the last 7 days, excluding node_modules
find . -type f -mtime -7 -not -path '*/node_modules/*'

# fd: same thing
fd -t f --changed-within 7d -E node_modules
fd is a fast, Rust-based alternative to find with opinionated defaults that match what people actually want 90% of the time:








Behavior
find
fd




Syntax
find . -iname '*pattern*'
fd pattern


Case sensitivity
Case-sensitive by default
Smart case (lowercase = insensitive)


Hidden files
Included
Skipped


.gitignore
Ignored
Respected automatically


Regex
-regex with full-path matching
Pattern is a regex by default, matched on filename


Parallel execution
-exec ... {} +
-x and -X run in parallel


Output color
None
Colorized, like ls


Empty pattern
Error
Lists everything



The big win is not raw speed (though it is fast) — it’s that the defaults are right. You type less, and you don’t accidentally grep through node_modules.
Two defaults are worth remembering, because they explain most “where did my file go?” moments:

Hidden entries are skipped. Add -H (or -u to also ignore .gitignore).
.gitignore is respected. Add -I, or -u for both.





The binary is called fd on macOS and Windows. (On Debian/Ubuntu it is packaged as fd-find and installed as fdfind — see the note at the end of this section.)


Homebrew (recommended):
brew install fd
MacPorts:
sudo port install fd
Cargo, if you already have a Rust toolchain:
cargo install fd-find
Prebuilt binary: download the macOS archive from the releases page, unpack it, and move fd somewhere on your PATH:
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
mv ~/Downloads/fd ~/.local/bin/
# make sure ~/.local/bin is on PATH (add to ~/.zshrc)
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
On Apple Silicon, brew install fd is the least friction. It also gives you shell completions and man pages for free.



fd is a single static .exe, so any of these work.
winget (built into Windows 10/11):
winget install sharkdp.fd
Scoop:
scoop install fd
Chocolatey (admin PowerShell):
choco install fd
Cargo:
cargo install fd-find
WSL / Git Bash: if you live in a Unix-like shell on Windows, use the Linux instructions. In WSL:
sudo apt install fd-find
Manual: grab fd-v*-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip from the releases page, extract fd.exe, and put it in a folder that is on your PATH (for example C:\Tools\fd).

The fdfind gotcha: Debian and Ubuntu package the binary as fdfind to avoid a name clash with another package. If you’re on those distros, either call fdfind directly or add an alias:
alias fd='fdfind'
Every example in this post uses fd.




fd --version
# fd 10.5.0
If the command is not found on Windows, close and reopen your terminal so the updated PATH is picked up.
Optional but nice: generate shell completions.
# zsh
fd --gen-completions zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_fd"

# bash
fd --gen-completions bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/fd > /dev/null

# fish
fd --gen-completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/fd.fish

# PowerShell
fd --gen-completions powershell | Out-File -Append $PROFILE





Almost every fd invocation is:
fd [options] <pattern> [path...]

pattern is a regular expression matched against the filename (not the full path, unless you pass -p).
path is where to search. Omit it and fd searches the current directory recursively.
If you omit the pattern too, it matches everything.

fd                      # every file and directory below .
fd config               # names containing "config"
fd '^test_' tests/      # names starting with "test_" inside tests/
fd . src                # everything under src
A few notes that save time later:

Smart case: fd readme is case-insensitive, fd Readme is case-sensitive. Force either with -i / -s.
-F treats the pattern as a literal string. -g treats it as a glob. -p matches the full path instead of just the name.
Directories are printed with a trailing /, which is handy visually but matters when you pipe through cut.







# all Markdown files
fd -e md

# several extensions at once
fd -e jpg -e jpeg -e png

# names containing "config"
fd config

# exact-ish: names starting with "test_" and ending in .py
fd '^test_.*\.py$'

# literal string (no regex escaping)
fd -F 'foo[1].txt'

# glob syntax
fd -g '*.tsx'
fd -g 'src/**/*.css'

# match against the full path, not just the filename
fd -p 'components/.*\.tsx$'

# force case-insensitive / case-sensitive
fd -i readme
fd -s Readme

# PID files anywhere under /var
fd -p '\.pid$' /var



This is the number one source of confusion, so learn these three flags:
fd -H                 # include hidden files and directories
fd -I                 # ignore .gitignore / .ignore / .fdignore rules
fd -u                 # both (-H -I); "unrestricted"
Examples:
fd -H .env                    # find .env files
fd -u -t d cache              # cache dirs, even if gitignored
fd -H -e json                 # hidden JSON files, still respecting gitignore
fd -I -e log                  # logs that may be gitignored
One nuance: by default, fd only honors .gitignore when it detects a git repository. If you want gitignore rules applied outside a repo:
fd --no-require-git -e js



-E accepts a glob and beats every other ignore rule:
fd -E node_modules -E dist -E target
fd -e js -E '*.min.js'
fd -t f -E '.git' -E 'vendor'
--prune is different: it stops descending into directories that match your search pattern.
# do not walk into any directory called "build"
fd -t d --prune build



fd -t f        # regular files
fd -t d        # directories
fd -t l        # symlinks
fd -t x        # executables
fd -t e        # empty files and directories
fd -t s        # sockets
fd -t p        # named pipes

# combine types
fd -t f -t l               # files and symlinks
fd -t e -t d               # empty directories
fd -t e -t f               # empty files



# files larger than 100 MB
fd -t f --size +100M

# files smaller than 10 KB
fd -t f --size -10k

# exactly 1 MiB (binary units: ki, mi, gi, ti)
fd -t f --size 1mi

# modified within the last 3 days
fd -t f --changed-within 3d

# modified before a date
fd -t f --changed-before 2025-01-01

# older than two weeks
fd -t f --changed-before 2weeks

# files owned by a user or group
fd -t f --owner deploy
fd -t f --owner '!root'



fd -d 1                # only the current directory
fd -d 2                # two levels down
fd --min-depth 2       # skip the top level
fd --exact-depth 3     # only level 3



fd -1 package.json             # stop after the first match
fd --max-results 20 -e log     # cap the output
fd -q '\.env$' && echo "found" # no output, exit code only
fd -l -e zip                   # ls -l style details
fd -L -t l                     # follow symlinks while walking
-l is handy because it shows sizes, timestamps, and symlink targets:
fd -l --size +50M -t f





Directories are where fd shines, because find . -type d -name ... is a lot of typing.
# every directory
fd -t d

# only top-level project folders
fd -t d -d 1

# just the names, no trailing slash noise
fd -t d -d 1 --format '{/}'

# directories named "src", excluding noise
fd -t d src -E node_modules -E .git

# nested src folders, e.g. packages/*/src
fd -t d -p 'packages/[^/]+/src$'

# empty directories (safe to delete after review)
fd -t e -t d

# recently changed directories
fd -t d --changed-within 1d

# hidden directories, e.g. .config folders
fd -t d -H -d 2

# find the directory containing a file
fd -p 'src/main\.rs$' --format '{//}'
That last one is a great example of why --format exists: {//} gives you the parent directory only.
A practical one — list the top-level folders in a monorepo with their file counts:
for d in $(fd -t d -d 1); do
  printf '%-30s %s\n' "$d" "$(fd -t f . "$d" | wc -l)"
done
Or without a loop, using awk (see fd + awk):
fd -t f | awk -F/ 'NF>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn




fd does not need xargs for most jobs. It has two execution modes:








Flag
Behavior
Runs




-x, --exec
One command per result, in parallel
Many times


-X, --exec-batch
One command with all results as arguments
Once (possibly batched)








Placeholder
Expands to
Example path
Result




{}
Full path
src/app.tsx
src/app.tsx


{/}
Basename
src/app.tsx
app.tsx


{//}
Parent directory
src/app.tsx
src


{.}
Path without extension
src/app.tsx
src/app


{/.}
Basename without extension
src/app.tsx
app



If you don’t include a placeholder, {} is appended automatically.



# line counts for every Markdown file (parallel)
fd -e md -x wc -l

# one wc call for all files, plus a total line
fd -e md -X wc -l

# unzip each archive into a folder named after the archive
fd -e zip -x unzip {} -d {/.}

# convert JPG to WebP next to the original
fd -e jpg -x magick {} {.}.webp

# format only changed TypeScript files
fd -e ts --changed-within 2d -x prettier --write {}

# gofmt all Go files in one shot
fd -e go -X gofmt -w

# make every shell script executable
fd -t f -e sh -x chmod +x

# find old logs, print the delete command first (dry run)
fd -e log --changed-before 30d -x echo rm {}

# then actually delete
fd -e log --changed-before 30d -x rm {}

# copy every PNG into one folder (careful with duplicate names)
fd -e png -x cp {} ~/Pictures/all/

# one shell per file, with proper quoting
fd -e png -x sh -c 'cp "$1" "$HOME/backup/$(basename "$1")"' _ {}
Two important behaviors:

Parallelism means unordered output. Use -j 1 (or --threads 1) if order matters.
-x and -X prefix paths with ./. That prevents a filename starting with - from being read as a flag. Strip it with --strip-cwd-prefix:

fd -e md -x wc -l | sort -k1 -n
#        0 ./README.md
#       12 ./docs/intro.md

fd -e md --strip-cwd-prefix -x wc -l | sort -k1 -n
#        0 README.md
#       12 docs/intro.md



Use -0 whenever filenames might contain spaces or newlines:
fd -0 -e md | xargs -0 wc -l
fd -0 -t f -e png | xargs -0 -n 20 pngquant --force --ext .png
fd -0 -e log | xargs -0 -I{} sh -c 'gzip "{}"'
xargs is still worth knowing for tools that read from stdin or for splitting work into batches (-n, -P). But if -x/-X can do the job, prefer them: they handle quoting correctly and skip the extra process.





fzf is a fuzzy filter for any list. fd produces a great list. Together they replace most GUI file pickers.
Install fzf:
# macOS
brew install fzf

# Windows
winget install junegunn.fzf
# or: scoop install fzf


fd | fzf
That’s it. Start typing part of a path; fzf narrows the list.



# plain preview
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'head -60 {}'

# with bat, if installed
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'bat --style=numbers --color=always --line-range=:80 {}'

# works with or without bat
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {} 2>/dev/null || head -60 {}'



fd -t d | fzf --preview 'ls -la {}'
fd -t d -d 2 | fzf --height 50% --preview 'eza --tree --level=2 {} 2>/dev/null || ls -la {}'



# single file
vim "$(fd -t f -e md | fzf)"

# VS Code
code "$(fd -t f -e tsx | fzf)"

# multi-select, robust against spaces in names
fd -t f -e tsx | fzf -m --print0 | xargs -0 code

# multi-select into vim
fd -t f -e md | fzf -m --print0 | xargs -0 vim



Add this to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc:
fcd() {
  local dir
  dir=$(fd -t d -H --exclude .git | fzf --height 40% --reverse) || return
  cd "$dir" || return
}
Then:
fcd
For old-school Ctrl+T / Alt+C behavior, fzf’s shell integration already provides file and directory picking. Modern fzf uses its built-in walker, but you can hand it fd explicitly when you want filtering:
# ~/.zshrc
export FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND='fd --type f --hidden --follow --exclude .git'
export FZF_CTRL_T_COMMAND="$FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND"
export FZF_ALT_C_COMMAND='fd --type d --hidden --follow --exclude .git'



The real power move is using fd’s filters to make the fuzzy list tiny:
# only files changed this week
fd -t f --changed-within 7d | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}'

# only files larger than 10 MB
fd -t f --size +10M | fzf

# only images, multi-select, copy picks into a folder
fd -t f -e jpg -e png -e webp |
  fzf -m --print0 |
  xargs -0 -I{} cp "{}" ~/Pictures/picks/

# only Markdown in docs/, open the chosen one in $PAGER
fd -e md . docs | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}' | xargs -r less

# pick a branch's changed files (requires git)
git diff --name-only | fzf --preview 'git diff -- {}'



# usage: fe [pattern]
fe() {
  local file
  file=$(fd -t f -H "${1:-}" | fzf --height 40% --reverse \
    --preview 'bat --color=always --line-range=:80 {} 2>/dev/null || head -40 {}') || return
  ${EDITOR:-vim} "$file"
}

# usage: fcp — pick one file, copy its path to the clipboard (macOS)
fcp() {
  fd -t f | fzf | pbcopy
}

# usage: fcdp — pick a file, jump to its directory
fcdp() {
  local f
  f=$(fd -t f | fzf) && cd "$(dirname "$f")"
}



Same idea in PowerShell:
fd | fzf
fd -e md | fzf --preview 'Get-Content {} -TotalCount 40'
If you use Git Bash or WSL, all of the Unix examples work unchanged.





awk turns a list of paths into answers: counts, sizes, depths, reports.


fd -t f | awk -F. 'NF>1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Output:
   34 tsx
   21 ts
    8 json
    3 md



stat differs by OS. On macOS:
fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -f%z | awk '{sum += $1} END {printf "%.1f MB\n", sum/1048576}'
On Linux:
fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -c%s | awk '{sum += $1} END {printf "%.1f MB\n", sum/1048576}'



fd -t f |
  awk -F/ 'NF>1 {d=$0; sub("/[^/]+$", "", d); c[d]++}
           END {for (d in c) print c[d], d}' |
  sort -rn |
  head -10
Output:
214 src/components
 88 src/utils
 41 tests



fd -t f | awk -F/ '{print NF-1}' | sort -n | uniq -c
  120 0    # top-level files
  340 1
  210 2
   45 3



fd -t f | awk -F/ '{print NF-1, $0}' | sort -rn | head -5



fd -t f -e png | awk -F/ '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -d



fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -f '%N,%z' | awk -F, '{printf "%s,%d\n", $1, $2}' > videos.csv



fd -e jpeg | awk '{print $0 " -> " $0 ".bak"}'
Then pipe the pairs into while read if you want to actually rename:
fd -e jpeg | awk '{print $0 " " $0 ".bak"}' | while read -r from to; do
  mv -- "$from" "$to"
done



# files whose path has at least 3 segments (i.e. under a subdirectory)
fd -t f | awk -F/ 'NF>=3'

Watch out: paths with spaces break naive awk '{print $2}' field access. If spaces are possible, use a delimiter that can’t appear in paths (like -0 + xargs, or stat with a tab separator), or parse from the left with -F/ as above.






cut is the blunt instrument for fixed-position fields: split on a delimiter, take a field. That makes it excellent for path segments and a poor fit for extensions (a name like Button.test.tsx has more than one dot). Use awk for the extension case; reach for cut when you’re already slicing paths.


fd -t f | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Note that top-level files also show up, each as its own single-item group. Filter to paths with a slash first:
fd -t f | grep / | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn



fd -t f -e tsx | cut -d/ -f2 | sort -u



fd -t d prints src/, so cut -d/ -f1 already strips the slash:
fd -t d -d 1 | cut -d/ -f1



fd -t f -d 1 | cut -d. -f2 | sort -u



fd -t f . src | cut -c5-



fd -t f | rev | cut -d/ -f1 | rev
fd -t f | sed 's|.*/||'            # simpler, same result
fd -t f --format '{/}'             # best: no external tools
That last line is the lesson: if fd can already do it with --format, you don’t need cut. Use cut when you’re already in a pipeline with other tools.







fd -t f | sort
fd -t f | sort -r



# macOS / Linux (du -k is portable enough)
fd -t f | xargs du -k | sort -rn | head -10
Using -x:
fd -t f -x du -k | sort -rn | head -10



# macOS
fd -t f -x stat -f '%m %N' | sort -rn | head -10

# Linux
fd -t f -x stat -c '%Y %n' | sort -rn | head -10
Human-readable dates, macOS:
fd -t f -x stat -f '%Sm %N' | sort -r | head -10



fd -t f -x du -h | sort -rh | head -20
Note: sort -h is GNU and also available in modern macOS sort. If yours complains, sort by kilobytes instead.



fd -e ts -e tsx -x wc -l | sort -k1 -nr | head -10



fd -t f | awk -F. 'NF>1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn



comm -12 \
  <(fd -t f . v1 | sed 's|^v1/||' | sort) \
  <(fd -t f . v2 | sed 's|^v2/||' | sort)



fd -t f | wc -l
fd -t f -e java | wc -l







# grep inside every Python file
fd -e py -x grep -n 'TODO' {}

# ripgrep already respects gitignore, but fd lets you pre-filter
fd -e ts -e tsx -0 | xargs -0 rg -n 'deprecated'



# macOS requires an empty backup suffix for -i
fd -e md -X sed -i '' 's/old-domain.com/new-domain.com/g'

# GNU sed
fd -e md -X sed -i 's/old-domain.com/new-domain.com/g'



# archive every log file, reading the list from stdin
fd -e log | tar -czf logs.tar.gz -T -

# safer with null separators
fd -0 -e log | tar -czf logs.tar.gz --null -T -



fd -t f -e jpg --changed-within 7d |
  rsync -av --files-from=- . /Volumes/Backup/photos/



fd -e png | parallel 'convert {} {.}.webp'
fd -e mp4 | parallel -j 4 'ffmpeg -i {} -vf scale=1280:-2 {.}-720p.mp4'



# stage every changed TypeScript file
fd -e ts --changed-within 1d | xargs git add

# find files that are tracked but deleted
comm -13 <(git ls-files | sort) <(fd -t f | sort)



# macOS
fd -e pdf -1 | xargs open

# Linux
fd -e pdf -1 | xargs xdg-open

# Windows PowerShell
fd -e pdf -1 | ForEach-Object { Start-Process $_ }



fd -e py -X wc -l | tail -1



# dry run, then execute
fd -t f -e sh -x echo chmod +x {}
fd -t f -e sh -x chmod +x {}

fd -t e -t f -x echo rm {}



fd -t d -d 1 | sed 's|/$||' | sed 's|^|/|' > .fdignore





This is where fd stops being a search tool and becomes a small static-site generator.


{
  echo "# Repository index"
  echo
  echo "Generated on $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
  echo
  fd -t f -E node_modules -E .git | sort | sed 's|^|- [ ] |'
} > INDEX.md
Result:
# Repository index

Generated on 2026-11-14

- [ ] README.md
- [ ] package.json
- [ ] src/app.tsx
- [ ] src/components/Button.tsx
Swap - [ ] for - [x] to make a checklist, or use plain - for a list.



{

  echo "| --- | ---: |"
  fd -t f -e tsx -x wc -l |
    awk '{gsub(/^\.\//, "", $2); printf "| `%s` | %d |\n", $2, $1}'
} > TSX-TABLE.md

| File | Lines |
| --- | ---: |
| `src/app.tsx` | 0 |
| `src/components/Button.tsx` | 0 |
If filenames may contain spaces, use fd --format to produce the path and stat for the metric instead, or quote the field with a separator that cannot appear in a path.



{
  echo "# Photo gallery"
  echo
  fd -t f -e jpg -e jpeg -e png -e webp | sort | sed 's|.*|![](<&>)|'
} > GALLERY.md
The <...> around the path is valid Markdown and survives spaces in filenames.



{
  echo "# Docs"
  echo
  fd -t f -e md . docs | sort | sed -E 's|^docs/(.*)\.md$|- [\1](\1.md)|'
} > docs/README.md



{
  echo "| Path | Size | Modified |"
  echo "| --- | ---: | --- |"
  fd -t f -x stat -f '%N|%z|%Sm' |
    sed 's|^\./||' |
    awk -F'|' '{printf "| `%s` | %s B | %s |\n", $1, $2, $3}'
} > INVENTORY.md
(Linux: replace stat -f '%N|%z|%Sm' with stat -c '%n|%s|%y'.)



fd -t d -d 1 |
  while read -r dir; do
    name=$(basename "$dir")
    [ -f "$dir/README.md" ] && continue
    printf '# %s\n\nFiles:\n\n' "$name" > "$dir/README.md"
    fd -t f . "$dir" | sed 's|^|- |' >> "$dir/README.md"
  done



Pair fd with comm and emit a Markdown table:
{
  echo "| Source | Test |"
  echo "| --- | --- |"
  fd -t f -e ts . src | while read -r src; do
    test_file="tests/$(basename "${src%.ts}").test.ts"
    [ -f "$test_file" ] || printf '| `%s` | missing |\n' "$src"
  done
} > MISSING-TESTS.md



fd -t f -e md --changed-within 1d |
  sort |
  sed -E 's|^(.*)/([^/]+)\.md$|- [\2](\1/\2.md)|'





fd itself is cross-platform. The surrounding toolchain is not.


Windows prints \ separators by default. Normalize when you plan to pipe into Unix tools:
fd -e tsx --path-separator / src
--path-separator / is also useful when generating Markdown links on Windows.






Unix pipeline
PowerShell

fd \| Sort-Object

# total size in MB

  Measure-Object -Sum |
  ForEach-Object { "{0:N1} MB" -f ($_.Sum / 1MB) }

Git Bash — ships with Git for Windows and includes awk, cut, sort, sed, grep, and xargs. Most examples in this post work as written.
WSL — a real Linux userland. Install fd with sudo apt install fd-find and alias it.

In Git Bash:

Works exactly like macOS/Linux.



fd passes each result as a single argument, so spaces are safe. When you need shell features (redirection, pipes, %VAR%), wrap in cmd or PowerShell:
fd -e log -x powershell -NoProfile -Command "Compress-Archive -Path '{}' -DestinationPath '{}.zip'"
Prefer -X when the command is a plain executable; it avoids spawning a shell per file.

title: fd command
text:
find is powerful, portable, and almost universally installed. It is also exhausting to type:
# find: files modified in the last 7 days, excluding node_modules
find . -type f -mtime -7 -not -path '*/node_modules/*'

# fd: same thing
fd -t f --changed-within 7d -E node_modules
fd is a fast, Rust-based alternative to find with opinionated defaults that match what people actually want 90% of the time:








Behavior
find
fd




Syntax
find . -iname '*pattern*'
fd pattern


Case sensitivity
Case-sensitive by default
Smart case (lowercase = insensitive)


Hidden files
Included

Respected automatically


Regex

Pattern is a regex by default, matched on filename


Parallel execution
-exec ... {} +

Output color
None
Colorized, like ls


Empty pattern
Error
Lists everything



The big win is not raw speed (though it is fast) — it’s that the defaults are right. You type less, and you don’t accidentally grep through node_modules.
Two defaults are worth remembering, because they explain most “where did my file go?” moments:

Hidden entries are skipped. Add -H (or -u to also ignore .gitignore).
.gitignore is respected. Add -I, or -u for both.

title: fd command
text:
The binary is called fd on macOS and Windows. (On Debian/Ubuntu it is packaged as fd-find and installed as fdfind — see the note at the end of this section.)


Homebrew (recommended):
brew install fd
MacPorts:
sudo port install fd
Cargo, if you already have a Rust toolchain:
cargo install fd-find
Prebuilt binary: download the macOS archive from the releases page, unpack it, and move fd somewhere on your PATH:
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
mv ~/Downloads/fd ~/.local/bin/
# make sure ~/.local/bin is on PATH (add to ~/.zshrc)
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
On Apple Silicon, brew install fd is the least friction. It also gives you shell completions and man pages for free.



fd is a single static .exe, so any of these work.
winget (built into Windows 10/11):
winget install sharkdp.fd
Scoop:
scoop install fd
Chocolatey (admin PowerShell):
choco install fd
Cargo:
cargo install fd-find
WSL / Git Bash: if you live in a Unix-like shell on Windows, use the Linux instructions. In WSL:
sudo apt install fd-find
Manual: grab fd-v*-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip from the releases page, extract fd.exe, and put it in a folder that is on your PATH (for example C:\Tools\fd).

The fdfind gotcha: Debian and Ubuntu package the binary as fdfind to avoid a name clash with another package. If you’re on those distros, either call fdfind directly or add an alias:
alias fd='fdfind'
Every example in this post uses fd.




fd --version
# fd 10.5.0
If the command is not found on Windows, close and reopen your terminal so the updated PATH is picked up.
Optional but nice: generate shell completions.
# zsh
fd --gen-completions zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_fd"

# bash
fd --gen-completions bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/fd > /dev/null

# fish
fd --gen-completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/fd.fish

# PowerShell
fd --gen-completions powershell | Out-File -Append $PROFILE

title: fd command
text:
Almost every fd invocation is:
fd [options] <pattern> [path...]

pattern is a regular expression matched against the filename (not the full path, unless you pass -p).
path is where to search. Omit it and fd searches the current directory recursively.
If you omit the pattern too, it matches everything.

fd                      # every file and directory below .
fd config               # names containing "config"
fd '^test_' tests/      # names starting with "test_" inside tests/
fd . src                # everything under src
A few notes that save time later:

Smart case: fd readme is case-insensitive, fd Readme is case-sensitive. Force either with -i / -s.
-F treats the pattern as a literal string. -g treats it as a glob. -p matches the full path instead of just the name.
Directories are printed with a trailing /, which is handy visually but matters when you pipe through cut.

title: fd command
text:
# all Markdown files
fd -e md

# several extensions at once
fd -e jpg -e jpeg -e png

# names containing "config"
fd config

# exact-ish: names starting with "test_" and ending in .py
fd '^test_.*\.py$'

# literal string (no regex escaping)
fd -F 'foo[1].txt'

# glob syntax
fd -g '*.tsx'
fd -g 'src/**/*.css'

# match against the full path, not just the filename
fd -p 'components/.*\.tsx$'

# force case-insensitive / case-sensitive
fd -i readme
fd -s Readme

# PID files anywhere under /var
fd -p '\.pid$' /var



This is the number one source of confusion, so learn these three flags:
fd -H                 # include hidden files and directories
fd -I                 # ignore .gitignore / .ignore / .fdignore rules
fd -u                 # both (-H -I); "unrestricted"
Examples:
fd -H .env                    # find .env files
fd -u -t d cache              # cache dirs, even if gitignored
fd -H -e json                 # hidden JSON files, still respecting gitignore
fd -I -e log                  # logs that may be gitignored
One nuance: by default, fd only honors .gitignore when it detects a git repository. If you want gitignore rules applied outside a repo:
fd --no-require-git -e js



-E accepts a glob and beats every other ignore rule:
fd -E node_modules -E dist -E target
fd -e js -E '*.min.js'
fd -t f -E '.git' -E 'vendor'
--prune is different: it stops descending into directories that match your search pattern.
# do not walk into any directory called "build"
fd -t d --prune build



fd -t f        # regular files
fd -t d        # directories
fd -t l        # symlinks
fd -t x        # executables
fd -t e        # empty files and directories
fd -t s        # sockets
fd -t p        # named pipes

# combine types
fd -t f -t l               # files and symlinks
fd -t e -t d               # empty directories
fd -t e -t f               # empty files



# files larger than 100 MB
fd -t f --size +100M

# files smaller than 10 KB
fd -t f --size -10k

# exactly 1 MiB (binary units: ki, mi, gi, ti)
fd -t f --size 1mi

# modified within the last 3 days
fd -t f --changed-within 3d

# modified before a date
fd -t f --changed-before 2025-01-01

# older than two weeks
fd -t f --changed-before 2weeks

# files owned by a user or group
fd -t f --owner deploy
fd -t f --owner '!root'



fd -d 1                # only the current directory
fd -d 2                # two levels down
fd --min-depth 2       # skip the top level
fd --exact-depth 3     # only level 3



fd -1 package.json             # stop after the first match
fd --max-results 20 -e log     # cap the output
fd -q '\.env$' && echo "found" # no output, exit code only
fd -l -e zip                   # ls -l style details
fd -L -t l                     # follow symlinks while walking
-l is handy because it shows sizes, timestamps, and symlink targets:
fd -l --size +50M -t f

title: fd command
text:
Directories are where fd shines, because find . -type d -name ... is a lot of typing.
# every directory
fd -t d

# only top-level project folders
fd -t d -d 1

# just the names, no trailing slash noise
fd -t d -d 1 --format '{/}'

# directories named "src", excluding noise
fd -t d src -E node_modules -E .git

# nested src folders, e.g. packages/*/src
fd -t d -p 'packages/[^/]+/src$'

# empty directories (safe to delete after review)
fd -t e -t d

# recently changed directories
fd -t d --changed-within 1d

# hidden directories, e.g. .config folders
fd -t d -H -d 2

# find the directory containing a file
fd -p 'src/main\.rs$' --format '{//}'
That last one is a great example of why --format exists: {//} gives you the parent directory only.
A practical one — list the top-level folders in a monorepo with their file counts:
for d in $(fd -t d -d 1); do
  printf '%-30s %s\n' "$d" "$(fd -t f . "$d" | wc -l)"
done
Or without a loop, using awk (see fd + awk):
fd -t f | awk -F/ 'NF>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

fd does not need xargs for most jobs. It has two execution modes:








Flag
Behavior
Runs




-x, --exec
One command per result, in parallel
Many times


-X, --exec-batch
One command with all results as arguments
Once (possibly batched)








Placeholder
Expands to
Example path
Result




{}
Full path
src/app.tsx
src/app.tsx


{/}
Basename
src/app.tsx
app.tsx


{//}
Parent directory
src/app.tsx
src


{.}
Path without extension
src/app.tsx
src/app


{/.}
Basename without extension
src/app.tsx
app



If you don’t include a placeholder, {} is appended automatically.



# line counts for every Markdown file (parallel)
fd -e md -x wc -l

# one wc call for all files, plus a total line
fd -e md -X wc -l

# unzip each archive into a folder named after the archive
fd -e zip -x unzip {} -d {/.}

# convert JPG to WebP next to the original
fd -e jpg -x magick {} {.}.webp

# format only changed TypeScript files
fd -e ts --changed-within 2d -x prettier --write {}

# gofmt all Go files in one shot
fd -e go -X gofmt -w

# make every shell script executable
fd -t f -e sh -x chmod +x

# find old logs, print the delete command first (dry run)
fd -e log --changed-before 30d -x echo rm {}

# then actually delete
fd -e log --changed-before 30d -x rm {}

# copy every PNG into one folder (careful with duplicate names)
fd -e png -x cp {} ~/Pictures/all/

# one shell per file, with proper quoting
fd -e png -x sh -c 'cp "$1" "$HOME/backup/$(basename "$1")"' _ {}
Two important behaviors:

Parallelism means unordered output. Use -j 1 (or --threads 1) if order matters.
-x and -X prefix paths with ./. That prevents a filename starting with - from being read as a flag. Strip it with --strip-cwd-prefix:

fd -e md -x wc -l | sort -k1 -n
#        0 ./README.md
#       12 ./docs/intro.md

fd -e md --strip-cwd-prefix -x wc -l | sort -k1 -n
#        0 README.md
#       12 docs/intro.md



Use -0 whenever filenames might contain spaces or newlines:
fd -0 -e md | xargs -0 wc -l
fd -0 -t f -e png | xargs -0 -n 20 pngquant --force --ext .png
fd -0 -e log | xargs -0 -I{} sh -c 'gzip "{}"'
xargs is still worth knowing for tools that read from stdin or for splitting work into batches (-n, -P). But if -x/-X can do the job, prefer them: they handle quoting correctly and skip the extra process.

title: fd command
text:
fzf is a fuzzy filter for any list. fd produces a great list. Together they replace most GUI file pickers.
Install fzf:
# macOS
brew install fzf

# Windows
winget install junegunn.fzf
# or: scoop install fzf


fd | fzf
That’s it. Start typing part of a path; fzf narrows the list.



# plain preview
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'head -60 {}'

# with bat, if installed
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'bat --style=numbers --color=always --line-range=:80 {}'

# works with or without bat
fd -t f | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {} 2>/dev/null || head -60 {}'



fd -t d | fzf --preview 'ls -la {}'
fd -t d -d 2 | fzf --height 50% --preview 'eza --tree --level=2 {} 2>/dev/null || ls -la {}'



# single file
vim "$(fd -t f -e md | fzf)"

# VS Code
code "$(fd -t f -e tsx | fzf)"

# multi-select, robust against spaces in names
fd -t f -e tsx | fzf -m --print0 | xargs -0 code

# multi-select into vim
fd -t f -e md | fzf -m --print0 | xargs -0 vim



Add this to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc:
fcd() {
  local dir
  dir=$(fd -t d -H --exclude .git | fzf --height 40% --reverse) || return
  cd "$dir" || return
}
Then:
fcd
For old-school Ctrl+T / Alt+C behavior, fzf’s shell integration already provides file and directory picking. Modern fzf uses its built-in walker, but you can hand it fd explicitly when you want filtering:
# ~/.zshrc
export FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND='fd --type f --hidden --follow --exclude .git'
export FZF_CTRL_T_COMMAND="$FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND"
export FZF_ALT_C_COMMAND='fd --type d --hidden --follow --exclude .git'



The real power move is using fd’s filters to make the fuzzy list tiny:
# only files changed this week
fd -t f --changed-within 7d | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}'

# only files larger than 10 MB
fd -t f --size +10M | fzf

# only images, multi-select, copy picks into a folder
fd -t f -e jpg -e png -e webp |
  fzf -m --print0 |
  xargs -0 -I{} cp "{}" ~/Pictures/picks/

# only Markdown in docs/, open the chosen one in $PAGER
fd -e md . docs | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}' | xargs -r less

# pick a branch's changed files (requires git)
git diff --name-only | fzf --preview 'git diff -- {}'



# usage: fe [pattern]
fe() {
  local file
  file=$(fd -t f -H "${1:-}" | fzf --height 40% --reverse \
    --preview 'bat --color=always --line-range=:80 {} 2>/dev/null || head -40 {}') || return
  ${EDITOR:-vim} "$file"
}

# usage: fcp — pick one file, copy its path to the clipboard (macOS)
fcp() {
  fd -t f | fzf | pbcopy
}

# usage: fcdp — pick a file, jump to its directory
fcdp() {
  local f
  f=$(fd -t f | fzf) && cd "$(dirname "$f")"
}



Same idea in PowerShell:
fd | fzf
fd -e md | fzf --preview 'Get-Content {} -TotalCount 40'
If you use Git Bash or WSL, all of the Unix examples work unchanged.

title: fd command
text:
awk turns a list of paths into answers: counts, sizes, depths, reports.


fd -t f | awk -F. 'NF>1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Output:
   34 tsx
   21 ts
    8 json
    3 md



stat differs by OS. On macOS:
fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -f%z | awk '{sum += $1} END {printf "%.1f MB\n", sum/1048576}'
On Linux:
fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -c%s | awk '{sum += $1} END {printf "%.1f MB\n", sum/1048576}'



fd -t f |
  awk -F/ 'NF>1 {d=$0; sub("/[^/]+$", "", d); c[d]++}
           END {for (d in c) print c[d], d}' |
  sort -rn |
  head -10
Output:
214 src/components
 88 src/utils
 41 tests



fd -t f | awk -F/ '{print NF-1}' | sort -n | uniq -c
  120 0    # top-level files
  340 1
  210 2
   45 3



fd -t f | awk -F/ '{print NF-1, $0}' | sort -rn | head -5



fd -t f -e png | awk -F/ '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -d



fd -t f -e mp4 -x stat -f '%N,%z' | awk -F, '{printf "%s,%d\n", $1, $2}' > videos.csv



fd -e jpeg | awk '{print $0 " -> " $0 ".bak"}'
Then pipe the pairs into while read if you want to actually rename:
fd -e jpeg | awk '{print $0 " " $0 ".bak"}' | while read -r from to; do
  mv -- "$from" "$to"
done



# files whose path has at least 3 segments (i.e. under a subdirectory)
fd -t f | awk -F/ 'NF>=3'

Watch out: paths with spaces break naive awk '{print $2}' field access. If spaces are possible, use a delimiter that can’t appear in paths (like -0 + xargs, or stat with a tab separator), or parse from the left with -F/ as above.

title: fd command
text:
cut is the blunt instrument for fixed-position fields: split on a delimiter, take a field. That makes it excellent for path segments and a poor fit for extensions (a name like Button.test.tsx has more than one dot). Use awk for the extension case; reach for cut when you’re already slicing paths.


fd -t f | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Note that top-level files also show up, each as its own single-item group. Filter to paths with a slash first:
fd -t f | grep / | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn



fd -t f -e tsx | cut -d/ -f2 | sort -u



fd -t d prints src/, so cut -d/ -f1 already strips the slash:
fd -t d -d 1 | cut -d/ -f1



fd -t f -d 1 | cut -d. -f2 | sort -u



fd -t f . src | cut -c5-



fd -t f | rev | cut -d/ -f1 | rev
fd -t f | sed 's|.*/||'            # simpler, same result
fd -t f --format '{/}'             # best: no external tools
That last line is the lesson: if fd can already do it with --format, you don’t need cut. Use cut when you’re already in a pipeline with other tools.

title: fd command
text:
This is where fd stops being a search tool and becomes a small static-site generator.


{
  echo "# Repository index"
  echo
  echo "Generated on $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
  echo
  fd -t f -E node_modules -E .git | sort | sed 's|^|- [ ] |'
} > INDEX.md
Result:
# Repository index

Generated on 2026-11-14

- [ ] README.md
- [ ] package.json
- [ ] src/app.tsx
- [ ] src/components/Button.tsx
Swap - [ ] for - [x] to make a checklist, or use plain - for a list.



{
  echo "| File | Lines |"
  echo "| --- | ---: |"
  fd -t f -e tsx -x wc -l |
    awk '{gsub(/^\.\//, "", $2); printf "| `%s` | %d |\n", $2, $1}'
} > TSX-TABLE.md
Result:
| File | Lines |
| --- | ---: |
| `src/app.tsx` | 0 |
| `src/components/Button.tsx` | 0 |
If filenames may contain spaces, use fd --format to produce the path and stat for the metric instead, or quote the field with a separator that cannot appear in a path.



{
  echo "# Photo gallery"
  echo
  fd -t f -e jpg -e jpeg -e png -e webp | sort | sed 's|.*|![](<&>)|'
} > GALLERY.md
The <...> around the path is valid Markdown and survives spaces in filenames.



{
  echo "# Docs"
  echo
  fd -t f -e md . docs | sort | sed -E 's|^docs/(.*)\.md$|- [\1](\1.md)|'
} > docs/README.md



{
  echo "| Path | Size | Modified |"
  echo "| --- | ---: | --- |"
  fd -t f -x stat -f '%N|%z|%Sm' |
    sed 's|^\./||' |
    awk -F'|' '{printf "| `%s` | %s B | %s |\n", $1, $2, $3}'
} > INVENTORY.md
(Linux: replace stat -f '%N|%z|%Sm' with stat -c '%n|%s|%y'.)



fd -t d -d 1 |
  while read -r dir; do
    name=$(basename "$dir")
    [ -f "$dir/README.md" ] && continue
    printf '# %s\n\nFiles:\n\n' "$name" > "$dir/README.md"
    fd -t f . "$dir" | sed 's|^|- |' >> "$dir/README.md"
  done



Pair fd with comm and emit a Markdown table:
{
  echo "| Source | Test |"
  echo "| --- | --- |"
  fd -t f -e ts . src | while read -r src; do
    test_file="tests/$(basename "${src%.ts}").test.ts"
    [ -f "$test_file" ] || printf '| `%s` | missing |\n' "$src"
  done
} > MISSING-TESTS.md



fd -t f -e md --changed-within 1d |
  sort |
  sed -E 's|^(.*)/([^/]+)\.md$|- [\2](\1/\2.md)|'

title: fd command
text:
fd itself is cross-platform. The surrounding toolchain is not.


Windows prints \ separators by default. Normalize when you plan to pipe into Unix tools:
fd -e tsx --path-separator / src
--path-separator / is also useful when generating Markdown links on Windows.






Unix pipeline
PowerShell




fd \| head -10
fd \| Select-Object -First 10


fd \| sort
fd \| Sort-Object


fd \| wc -l
fd \| Measure-Object -Line


fd \| xargs rm
fd \| ForEach-Object { Remove-Item $_ }


fd \| grep foo
fd \| Select-String foo


fd -x wc -l
fd -x wc -l (if Git’s Unix tools are on PATH)



Examples:
# ten most recently modified files
fd -t f | Get-Item | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 10

# count files per extension
fd -t f | Get-Item | Group-Object Extension | Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Select-Object Count, Name

# open a fuzzy-picked file
fd -t f -e md | fzf | ForEach-Object { code $_ }

# total size in MB
fd -t f | ForEach-Object { (Get-Item $_).Length } |
  Measure-Object -Sum |
  ForEach-Object { "{0:N1} MB" -f ($_.Sum / 1MB) }



Two good options:

Git Bash — ships with Git for Windows and includes awk, cut, sort, sed, grep, and xargs. Most examples in this post work as written.
WSL — a real Linux userland. Install fd with sudo apt install fd-find and alias it.

In Git Bash:
fd -t f | awk -F. 'NF>1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Works exactly like macOS/Linux.



fd passes each result as a single argument, so spaces are safe. When you need shell features (redirection, pipes, %VAR%), wrap in cmd or PowerShell:
fd -e log -x powershell -NoProfile -Command "Compress-Archive -Path '{}' -DestinationPath '{}.zip'"
Prefer -X when the command is a plain executable; it avoids spawning a shell per file.

title: fd command
text:
fd is one of those tools that looks like a small quality-of-life upgrade and quietly changes how you work. The pattern is always the same: narrow with fd, then hand the list to something else.

Narrow with -t, -e, -d, -S, --changed-within.
Explore interactively with fzf --preview.
Summarize with awk, cut, sort, uniq.
Act with -x, -X, or xargs -0.
Ship the result as Markdown with a tiny { ... } > FILE.md block.

Learn five flags this week — -t, -e, -d, -H, -x — and you’ll rarely reach for find again.
